questions.stem: For the chi-square test of the data in the table, why are there 3 degrees of freedom?
choices: There are three phenotypes that differ from the parents.
Three of the four observed values differ from the expected values.
There are four phenotype classes, and the number of degrees of freedom is one less than the number of classes.
There are two genes with two alleles each, minus one.
questions.explanation: Once the total number of offspring is fixed, the counts in three of the four classes determine the count in the fourth, so only three values are free to vary. For a test of goodness of fit, the degrees of freedom equal the number of categories minus one.

questions.stem: A fruit fly heterozygous for body color and wing shape was crossed with a fly homozygous recessive for both traits, with the results shown. Which is the best estimate of the distance between the two genes?
choices: 9.75 map units
39 map units
50 map units
19.5 map units
questions.explanation: The two rare classes, 98 and 97 flies, are recombinants produced by crossing over between the genes. The recombination frequency is \(\dfrac{195}{1000}=19.5\%\), and one map unit corresponds to a recombination frequency of 1%.

questions.stem: Why do the data in the table differ from the 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio expected for a testcross involving two genes?
choices: The genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
One of the alleles is lethal when homozygous.
The genes are on the same chromosome, so the parental combinations of alleles are inherited together unless crossing over occurs between them.
The two genes interact so that one masks the expression of the other.
questions.explanation: Independent assortment would give four equally frequent classes. Here the two parental combinations make up about 80% of the offspring, which shows the genes are linked. The less frequent classes arise from crossing over between homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.

questions.stem: Red-green color blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman who is a carrier and a man with normal color vision have a son who is color-blind and has the sex chromosomes XXY. Assuming no new mutation, in which parent and in which division did nondisjunction occur?
choices: In the mother, during meiosis I
In the mother, during meiosis II
In the father, during meiosis I
In the father, during meiosis II
questions.explanation: The son must have two X chromosomes carrying the recessive allele, and only the mother has that allele, so both came from her. They are copies of the same chromosome, which fail to separate when sister chromatids do not separate in meiosis II. Nondisjunction in her meiosis I would give the son one X with each allele and normal vision.

questions.stem: Two individuals with the genotype AaBbCc are crossed. The three genes assort independently, and at each gene the allele written in upper case is completely dominant. What is the probability that an offspring shows the dominant phenotype for gene A, the recessive phenotype for gene B, and is heterozygous for gene C?
questions.explanation: Because the genes assort independently, the probabilities multiply: \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) for the dominant phenotype of A, \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) for bb, and \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) for Cc. The product is \(\dfrac{3}{32}\).

questions.stem: Hemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman who is a carrier and a man who does not have hemophilia plan to have a child. What is the probability that the child will be a son with hemophilia?
questions.explanation: The probability that the child is a son is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), and the probability that a son inherits the mother's X chromosome with the recessive allele is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), giving \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). One half is the probability that a son, once it is known the child is a son, is affected.

questions.stem: A disorder that affects cells with high energy demands is caused by a mutation in mitochondrial DNA. Which pattern of inheritance is expected?
choices: All children of an affected mother can inherit the mutation, and no children of an affected father inherit it.
Half of the children of an affected parent of either sex inherit the mutation.
Only sons of an affected mother inherit the mutation.
Only daughters of an affected father inherit the mutation.
questions.explanation: Mitochondria in a zygote come almost entirely from the cytoplasm of the egg, so mitochondrial genes are inherited from the mother by sons and daughters alike. Sperm contribute essentially no mitochondria, so an affected father does not pass on the mutation.

questions.stem: Two Labrador retrievers that are heterozygous at two genes are crossed many times. Their puppies appear in a ratio of 9 black : 3 brown : 4 yellow. Which explanation best accounts for this ratio?
choices: The two genes are closely linked on the same chromosome.
Coat color is controlled by a single gene with incomplete dominance.
Yellow puppies result from a new mutation in each generation.
One gene is epistatic: a homozygous recessive genotype at one gene prevents the pigment specified by the other gene from being deposited.
questions.explanation: A 9 : 3 : 4 ratio is a modified 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio, which shows two independently assorting genes. The last two classes are combined because dogs homozygous recessive at the gene controlling pigment deposition are yellow regardless of their genotype at the pigment-color gene.

questions.stem: Himalayan rabbits have white fur on the body and black fur on the ears, nose, feet, and tail. When a patch of white fur on a rabbit's back is shaved and an ice pack is kept on the area, the fur that grows back is black. Which statement best explains the result?
choices: The cold causes a mutation in the pigment gene in the skin cells.
The enzyme that makes the pigment is active only at lower temperatures, so the phenotype depends on the environment as well as the genotype.
The cells on the rabbit's back have different alleles from the cells of the ears.
The cold kills the white-fur cells, and black-fur cells migrate into the area.
questions.explanation: Every cell of the rabbit has the same alleles, but the enzyme they encode is temperature sensitive and works only in cooler regions of the body. Cooling the back allows the enzyme to function there. The same genotype can produce different phenotypes in different environments.

questions.stem: The pedigree shows a rare disorder; filled symbols represent affected individuals. Which mode of inheritance is most consistent with the pedigree?
choices: Autosomal dominant
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Y-linked
questions.explanation: The trait skips a generation: an affected grandfather has an unaffected daughter whose son is affected, and only males are affected. An affected man passes his X chromosome to all of his daughters, who are carriers. X-linked dominant inheritance would make the daughter affected, and a Y-linked trait could not pass through her.

questions.stem: In the pedigree shown, the disorder is X-linked recessive. If individuals II-1 and II-2 have another son, what is the probability that he will be affected?
questions.explanation: II-1 received her father's X chromosome and must be a carrier. A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and one of his mother's two X chromosomes, so he has a one-half chance of receiving the X with the recessive allele. One fourth is the chance that the next child, of either sex, is an affected son.

questions.stem: The graph shows the amount of DNA per cell during meiosis. During which labeled interval do homologous chromosomes separate into different cells?
choices: Interval Y
Interval W
Interval X
Interval Z
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated during interval X. In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes separate and the DNA per cell halves, from 4 to 2 units, at Y. In meiosis II, sister chromatids separate and the DNA halves again, at Z.

questions.stem: Based on the graph, how does the DNA content of a gamete compare with that of a body cell of the same organism in G₁?
choices: It is the same.
It is one quarter as much.
It is half as much.
It is twice as much.
questions.explanation: A G₁ cell has 2 units of DNA in the graph and a gamete has 1. Replication doubles the DNA and two divisions halve it twice, so gametes are haploid and fertilization restores the diploid amount.

questions.stem: Students crossed two heterozygous plants and counted the offspring, as shown. Using \(\chi^2=\sum\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}\) and a critical value of 3.84 (1 degree of freedom, \(p=0.05\)), which conclusion is correct?
choices: \(\chi^2\approx 1.33\); the data are inconsistent with a 3 : 1 ratio.
\(\chi^2\approx 0.33\); the data are consistent with a 3 : 1 ratio.
\(\chi^2\approx 10\); the data are inconsistent with a 3 : 1 ratio.
\(\chi^2\approx 1.33\); the data are consistent with a 3 : 1 ratio.
questions.explanation: \(\chi^2=\dfrac{(70-75)^2}{75}+\dfrac{(30-25)^2}{25}=0.33+1.00=1.33\). This is below 3.84, so the deviation from 3 : 1 can be attributed to chance and the null hypothesis is not rejected. The value 0.33 comes from omitting the white class.

figure.alt: Table of 100 offspring: 70 purple-flowered observed, 75 expected; 30 white-flowered observed, 25 expected

questions.stem: Suppose the students had counted 700 purple-flowered and 300 white-flowered offspring, the same proportions as in the table. What would the chi-square test show?
choices: \(\chi^2\approx 1.33\), the same as before, because the proportions are the same.
\(\chi^2\approx 0.13\); the fit would be better because the sample is larger.
\(\chi^2\approx 13.3\); the deviation from 3 : 1 would be statistically significant.
The test cannot be applied to samples larger than 100.
questions.explanation: With expected values of 750 and 250, \(\chi^2=\dfrac{50^2}{750}+\dfrac{50^2}{250}=3.33+10=13.3\). A larger sample makes the same proportional deviation less likely to arise by chance, so it would justify rejecting the 3 : 1 hypothesis.

figure.alt: Table of recombination frequencies: genes A and B, 12 percent; genes B and C, 5 percent; genes A and C, 16 percent

questions.stem: The table shows recombination frequencies between three linked genes. What is the order of the genes on the chromosome?
choices: A, C, B
A, B, C
B, A, C
The order cannot be determined from recombination frequencies.
questions.explanation: Recombination frequency increases with distance, so the two genes farthest apart, A and C at 16 percent, are at the ends. Gene B lies between them, 12 map units from A and 5 from C.

figure.alt: Table of recombination frequencies: genes A and B, 12 percent; genes B and C, 5 percent; genes A and C, 16 percent

questions.stem: In the table, the recombination frequency between A and C is 16 percent, slightly less than the sum of the A–B and B–C frequencies. Which statement best explains the difference?
choices: Some chromosomes undergo two crossovers between A and C, which restore the parental combination of those two genes and go undetected.
Gene B interferes with crossing over between A and C.
Recombination frequencies cannot be added, because the genes are on different chromosomes.
Crossing over between A and C occurs only in males.
questions.explanation: A double crossover, one on each side of B, swaps the alleles twice and leaves A and C in their parental arrangement. Measuring A and C alone misses those events, so distant genes appear slightly closer than the sum of intervening distances.

questions.stem: A man with blood type AB and a woman with blood type O have a child. What is the probability that the child has blood type A?
questions.explanation: The man is \(I^AI^B\) and the woman is \(ii\). Every child receives \(i\) from the mother and \(I^A\) or \(I^B\) from the father with equal probability, so the children are type A (\(I^Ai\)) or type B (\(I^Bi\)), each with probability one half. No child can be AB or O.

questions.stem: Human height shows a continuous range of values that forms a bell-shaped distribution in a population. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?
choices: Height is influenced by many genes, each with a small additive effect, along with environmental factors such as nutrition.
Height is controlled by a single gene with two alleles showing incomplete dominance.
Height is determined entirely by the environment.
Height is controlled by one gene with many codominant alleles.
questions.explanation: When many genes each contribute a little, the number of possible genotypes is large and most people fall near the middle. Environmental effects blur the boundaries further, giving continuous variation rather than distinct classes.

questions.stem: How many genetically different kinds of gametes can be produced by an individual with the genotype AaBbCcDd, if the four genes assort independently?
questions.explanation: Each gene contributes one of two alleles to a gamete, and independent assortment makes every combination possible: \(2^4=16\). The number 81 is the number of genotypes possible among the offspring of two such individuals.

questions.stem: How do the gametes produced when a pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate in meiosis I compare with those produced when sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis II?
choices: Nondisjunction in meiosis I makes two of the four gametes abnormal; nondisjunction in meiosis II makes all four abnormal.
Nondisjunction in meiosis I makes all four gametes abnormal; nondisjunction in meiosis II makes two of the four abnormal.
Both produce two normal and two abnormal gametes.
Both make all four gametes abnormal.
questions.explanation: If homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, one daughter cell gets both and the other gets neither, so all four gametes are n + 1 or n − 1. In meiosis II, the failure occurs in only one of the two dividing cells, so the other cell's two gametes are normal.

questions.stem: Which process produces a chromosome carrying a combination of alleles that was not present on either chromosome of the parent?
choices: Independent assortment of homologous chromosomes in metaphase I
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I
Separation of sister chromatids in meiosis II
Random fertilization of an egg by a sperm
questions.explanation: Crossing over exchanges segments between homologs, creating recombinant chromosomes. Independent assortment and random fertilization produce new combinations of whole chromosomes, but each chromosome itself is unchanged.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the lac operon of E. coli in the absence of lactose. What happens when lactose becomes available and glucose is absent?
choices: Lactose binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.
Lactose binds RNA polymerase, allowing it to transcribe through the repressor.
The repressor binds lactose and then binds the operator more tightly.
A molecule derived from lactose binds the repressor, which changes shape and releases the operator, allowing transcription of the genes.
questions.explanation: The lac operon is inducible. Allolactose, an isomer of lactose, acts as the inducer by binding the repressor and changing its shape so that it can no longer bind the operator. RNA polymerase can then transcribe the genes for the enzymes that take up and digest lactose.

questions.stem: A mutation changes the operator of the lac operon shown so that the repressor can no longer bind to it. Which outcome is expected?
choices: The lac genes are transcribed whether or not lactose is present.
The lac genes are never transcribed.
The lac genes are transcribed only when lactose is present.
The repressor is no longer produced.
questions.explanation: The repressor turns the operon off by binding the operator. If it cannot bind, nothing blocks RNA polymerase, and the genes are expressed continuously, which is called constitutive expression. The cell wastes resources making enzymes when there is no lactose to digest.

figure.alt: Table of selected mRNA codons: AUG is methionine and the start codon, UUU is phenylalanine, UGG is tryptophan, UGA is a stop codon, CAU is histidine, GGU and GGC are both glycine

questions.stem: An mRNA has the sequence 5′-AUG UUU UGG CAU GGU-3′. A mutation in the gene changes the third codon from UGG to UGA. Based on the table, what is the effect on the polypeptide?
choices: Tryptophan is replaced by a different amino acid, and the rest of the polypeptide is unchanged.
The reading frame shifts, changing every amino acid after the second.
Translation stops after the second amino acid, producing a shortened polypeptide.
There is no effect, because the genetic code is redundant.
questions.explanation: UGA is a stop codon, so the ribosome releases the polypeptide after phenylalanine. A substitution that creates a stop codon is a nonsense mutation and usually yields a nonfunctional protein. A substitution does not shift the reading frame; that requires an insertion or deletion.

figure.alt: Table of selected mRNA codons: AUG is methionine and the start codon, UUU is phenylalanine, UGG is tryptophan, UGA is a stop codon, CAU is histidine, GGU and GGC are both glycine

questions.stem: An mRNA has the sequence 5′-AUG UUU UGG CAU GGU-3′. A different mutation changes the last codon from GGU to GGC. Based on the table, what is the effect on the polypeptide?
choices: Glycine is replaced by another amino acid.
Translation ends one codon early.
The polypeptide is one amino acid longer.
There is no change in the amino acid sequence.
questions.explanation: GGU and GGC both code for glycine, so the mutation is silent. Because most amino acids are specified by more than one codon, many changes in the third position of a codon do not alter the protein.

choices: The DNA from the crime scene is consistent with suspect 1 only.
The DNA from the crime scene is consistent with all three suspects, because every lane has three bands.
The DNA from the crime scene is consistent with suspect 2 and excludes suspects 1 and 3.
No conclusion is possible, because the bands do not match the size marker.
questions.explanation: Fragments of the same length travel the same distance. Only suspect 2 has bands at all three positions found in the crime scene sample. Suspects 1 and 3 each share one band with it, which is expected by chance, but the other bands differ, which excludes them.

questions.stem: In the gel shown, why are the bands farthest from the wells made up of the shortest DNA fragments?
choices: Shorter fragments carry more negative charge per fragment than longer ones.
DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the positive electrode, and shorter fragments pass through the pores of the gel more easily.
DNA is positively charged, and shorter fragments are repelled more strongly by the wells.
Longer fragments are broken down by the electric current.
questions.explanation: The phosphate groups of DNA give every fragment a negative charge in proportion to its length, so all fragments are pulled toward the positive electrode. The gel acts as a sieve that slows long fragments more than short ones, separating them by size.

questions.stem: Bacteria that are sensitive to ampicillin are mixed with the plasmid shown and then spread on plates containing nutrient medium with ampicillin. A few colonies grow. Which statement best explains the result?
choices: Only the cells that took up the plasmid express the resistance gene and survive.
The ampicillin caused some cells to mutate and become resistant.
All of the cells took up the plasmid, but only some of them divided.
The cells that grew broke down the plasmid and used it as a nutrient.
questions.explanation: Transformation is inefficient, so only a small fraction of the cells take up a plasmid. Those cells make the product of the ampR gene, which inactivates ampicillin. The antibiotic selects for the transformed cells; it does not cause them to become resistant.

questions.stem: Bacteria were grown for many generations in a medium containing heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) and then moved to a medium containing light nitrogen (¹⁴N). DNA was extracted after each generation and centrifuged, with the results shown. Which model of DNA replication do the results support?
choices: Conservative: the original double helix stays intact and an entirely new double helix is made.
Dispersive: every strand is a mixture of original and new segments.
Semiconservative: each new double helix has one original strand and one new strand.
Semiconservative, but only for the first generation.
questions.explanation: After one generation all of the DNA is of intermediate density, which rules out the conservative model. After two generations there are two bands, hybrid and light, which rules out the dispersive model, because that model predicts a single band that becomes lighter each generation.

questions.stem: Nerve cells and liver cells of the same person contain the same genes but produce many different proteins. Which statement best explains how this is possible?
choices: The two cell types contain different sets of transcription factors, so different genes are transcribed.
Each cell type loses the genes it does not need during development.
The two cell types use different genetic codes to translate the same mRNAs.
Liver cells have more chromosomes than nerve cells.
questions.explanation: With rare exceptions, all somatic cells of an organism have the same genome. Differences among cell types arise from differential gene expression: the particular combination of activators and repressors in a cell determines which genes are transcribed.

questions.stem: In a tumor, the promoter of a gene that normally restrains cell division is found to be heavily methylated, although the DNA sequence of the gene is normal. Which effect of the methylation is most likely?
choices: The gene is transcribed at a higher rate than normal.
The amino acid sequence of the protein is altered.
The gene is deleted from the chromosome.
Transcription of the gene is reduced, so less of the protein is made.
questions.explanation: Methyl groups added to cytosines in a promoter are associated with tightly packed chromatin and reduced transcription. The gene is silenced even though its sequence is unchanged, which is an epigenetic change. Acetylation of histones has the opposite effect, loosening chromatin.

questions.stem: Researchers find that a small RNA molecule, a microRNA, is complementary to part of the mRNA of gene G. In cells that make the microRNA, transcription of gene G is normal, but very little of protein G is present. Which statement best explains the observation?
choices: The microRNA binds the promoter of gene G and blocks RNA polymerase.
The microRNA binds the mRNA of gene G, blocking its translation or marking it for degradation.
The microRNA changes the DNA sequence of gene G.
The microRNA is translated into a protein that competes with protein G.
questions.explanation: MicroRNAs base-pair with target mRNAs as part of a protein complex that prevents translation or degrades the mRNA. This regulates gene expression after transcription, which fits the observation that the gene is transcribed normally but little protein accumulates.

questions.stem: Which of the following mutations within the coding region of a gene is most likely to eliminate the function of the protein?
choices: Deletion of three consecutive nucleotides near the end of the coding region
Deletion of a single nucleotide near the beginning of the coding region
Substitution of one nucleotide in the third position of a codon
Substitution that replaces one nonpolar amino acid with another near the end of the protein
questions.explanation: Deleting one nucleotide shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is misread, and a stop codon usually appears early. When this happens near the start of the gene, almost the entire protein is wrong. Deleting three nucleotides removes one amino acid and leaves the rest of the sequence intact.

questions.stem: A mutation in intron 1 of the gene shown destroys a splice site, causing exon 2 to be skipped: exon 1 is joined directly to exon 3. Which effect on the protein is most likely?
choices: It lacks 30 amino acids, and the amino acids encoded by exon 3 are unchanged, because 90 is a multiple of 3.
Every amino acid encoded by exon 3 is changed, because the reading frame shifts.
It is longer, because intron 1 is now translated.
It is unchanged, because exon 2 is not part of the coding sequence.
questions.explanation: Removing 90 nucleotides removes 30 codons without shifting the reading frame. Skipping an exon whose length is not a multiple of three would shift the frame and alter everything downstream. Alternative splicing uses the same principle to make related proteins from one gene.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the trp operon when tryptophan is abundant. Which statement describes how the operon is regulated?
choices: Tryptophan binds the operator directly and blocks RNA polymerase.
Tryptophan removes the repressor from the operator, turning the genes on.
Tryptophan binds the repressor and activates it, so the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription.
The repressor binds tryptophan and destroys it.
questions.explanation: The trp operon is repressible: its repressor is inactive alone and becomes active when tryptophan, the end product of the pathway, binds it as a corepressor. The cell stops making the enzymes when it has enough of their product.

choices: The trp genes are never transcribed.
The trp genes are transcribed only when tryptophan is present.
The repressor binds the operator permanently.
The trp genes are transcribed whether or not tryptophan is present.
questions.explanation: Without tryptophan bound, the repressor stays in its inactive shape and cannot bind the operator. RNA polymerase transcribes the genes continuously, wasting energy on enzymes even when tryptophan is plentiful.

Three bands, of 3, 4, and 3 kb
Two bands: one of 3 kb and one of 2 kb, each containing two fragments
One band, because all of the fragments are the same length

choices: EcoRI alone
HindIII alone
EcoRI and HindIII together
Neither enzyme, because the molecule is linear
questions.explanation: HindIII cuts once at 5 kb, producing two fragments of 5 kb that run together. EcoRI alone produces fragments of 3, 4, and 3 kb, which give two bands.

questions.stem: The table shows β-galactosidase activity in E. coli grown in four media. Which statement best explains why activity is highest when lactose is present and glucose is absent?
choices: Lactose inactivates the repressor, and low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP and helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter.
Glucose activates the repressor, which binds lactose.
Lactose increases the amount of glucose in the cell, which activates transcription.
Without glucose, the cell makes more repressor, which activates transcription.
questions.explanation: The lac operon has two controls. Removing the repressor allows transcription, and the CAP–cAMP complex strongly increases it. Both conditions are met only when lactose is present and glucose is scarce, so the cell uses lactose only when its preferred sugar runs out.

figure.alt: Table of beta-galactosidase activity in E. coli grown in four media. Glucose present, lactose absent: 2 units. Glucose present, lactose present: 120. Glucose absent, lactose absent: 3. Glucose absent, lactose present: 1,500

questions.stem: A mutant strain of E. coli cannot make cAMP. In a medium with lactose and no glucose, what level of β-galactosidase activity is expected, based on the table?
choices: About 1,500 units, the same as the normal strain
About 2 units, because the repressor stays bound
Low, similar to the 120 units seen with both sugars present
Higher than 1,500 units, because the cell cannot sense glucose
questions.explanation: Lactose still removes the repressor, so some transcription occurs, but without cAMP, CAP cannot boost RNA polymerase binding. The result resembles the induced but CAP-free condition in which glucose keeps cAMP low.

questions.stem: A tRNA has the anticodon 3′-UAC-5′. Which mRNA codon does it pair with, and which amino acid does it carry?
choices: 5′-AUG-3′, methionine
5′-UAC-3′, tyrosine
5′-CAU-3′, histidine
5′-ATG-3′, methionine
questions.explanation: Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel: U pairs with A, A with U, and C with G, giving 5′-AUG-3′. AUG codes for methionine and is the start codon. mRNA contains uracil, not thymine.

questions.stem: A bacterial strain has a temperature-sensitive DNA ligase that stops working at high temperature. When the bacteria are shifted to high temperature during DNA replication, what accumulates?
choices: Unwound, single-stranded DNA with no new strands made
RNA primers that are never synthesized
Leading strands that are not extended
Short DNA fragments from the lagging strand that are not joined together
questions.explanation: The lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, whose RNA primers are replaced with DNA. Ligase seals the remaining gaps in the backbone; without it the fragments stay separate.

questions.stem: In most human somatic cells, chromosomes become slightly shorter with each round of DNA replication, but in germ cells and many cancer cells they do not. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Somatic cells lose a gene each time they divide.
Germ cells and many cancer cells make telomerase, which extends the repetitive sequences at chromosome ends.
DNA polymerase in germ cells can add nucleotides without a primer.
Cancer cells do not replicate their DNA before dividing.
questions.explanation: On the lagging strand, removing the final primer leaves a gap at the very end that DNA polymerase cannot fill, so the ends shorten. Telomerase carries its own RNA template and extends the telomeres, allowing unlimited divisions.

questions.stem: A scientist inserts a human gene, copied directly from genomic DNA, into a plasmid and expresses it in bacteria, but the protein produced is not functional. The same gene expressed in yeast works. Which change would most likely allow the bacteria to make a functional protein?
choices: Insert the gene into a second plasmid in the same bacteria.
Insert DNA made from the gene's mature mRNA by reverse transcriptase (cDNA) instead of the genomic DNA.
Grow the bacteria at a higher temperature.
Add the human promoter to the gene.
questions.explanation: Human genes contain introns, and bacteria lack the machinery to splice them out, so the transcript is translated with the introns included. cDNA made from processed mRNA already lacks introns. Yeast, as eukaryotes, can splice.

questions.stem: A drug inhibits the enzymes that remove acetyl groups from histone proteins. Which effect on gene expression is most likely in treated cells?
choices: Chromatin becomes more tightly packed, and transcription decreases.
The DNA sequence of many genes changes.
Translation of all mRNAs stops.
Chromatin becomes less tightly packed, and transcription of many genes increases.
questions.explanation: Acetylation neutralizes positive charges on histones, loosening their grip on DNA and making it accessible to transcription machinery. Blocking deacetylation keeps chromatin open, an epigenetic change that does not alter the DNA sequence.

figure.alt: Graph of number of birds versus beak depth. Before the drought the distribution is centered near 9 millimeters with a peak of 36 birds. The survivors of the drought form a smaller distribution centered near 10.2 millimeters

questions.stem: During a drought on an island, small soft seeds became scarce and mostly large, hard seeds remained. The graph shows the beak depths of a finch population before the drought and of the birds that survived it. Beak depth is heritable. Which statement best describes what happened?
choices: Directional selection: birds with deeper beaks were more likely to survive, so the average beak depth of the population increased.
Stabilizing selection: birds with average beaks were more likely to survive.
Disruptive selection: birds with the shallowest and the deepest beaks were more likely to survive.
Genetic drift: the survivors were a random sample of the original population.
questions.explanation: The survivors are not a random sample: their distribution is shifted toward deeper beaks, which can crack the large, hard seeds that remained. Selection that favors one extreme of a heritable trait shifts the population mean in that direction in later generations.

figure.alt: Graph of number of birds versus beak depth. Before the drought the distribution is centered near 9 millimeters with a peak of 36 birds. The survivors of the drought form a smaller distribution centered near 10.2 millimeters

questions.stem: A student summarizes the data in the graph by saying, "The finches grew deeper beaks because they needed them to crack the hard seeds." Which statement best corrects the student's claim?
choices: The birds changed their beaks through use, and the offspring inherited the change.
The drought caused mutations for deeper beaks in the birds that needed them.
Individual birds did not change; birds that already had deeper beaks survived and reproduced at a higher rate, changing the makeup of the population.
All of the birds had the same beak depth before the drought.
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on heritable variation that already exists. The environment does not produce the traits that are needed; it determines which existing variants leave more offspring. Populations evolve, while the traits of an individual bird stay the same.

questions.stem: In a population that is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of the individuals show a recessive phenotype. What percentage of the population is heterozygous?
questions.explanation: The recessive phenotype has frequency \(q^2=0.16\), so \(q=0.4\) and \(p=0.6\). The frequency of heterozygotes is \(2pq=2(0.6)(0.4)=0.48\). The remaining 36% are homozygous dominant.

figure.alt: Table of observed genotypes in a population of 1,000: 280 AA, 240 Aa, and 480 aa

questions.stem: The table shows the genotypes observed in a population. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, because both alleles are still present.
The population is not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, because the two alleles do not have equal frequencies.
The population is not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: there are half as many heterozygotes as expected, which is consistent with nonrandom mating.
The population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, because the genotype frequencies add up to 1.
questions.explanation: The frequency of allele A is \(\dfrac{2(280)+240}{2000}=0.4\), so \(q=0.6\). The expected number of heterozygotes is \(2pq(1000)=480\), but only 240 were observed. A deficit of heterozygotes is typical when individuals mate preferentially with others of the same genotype, as in inbreeding.

questions.stem: The graph shows the frequency of allele B in three populations in which the allele has no effect on survival or reproduction. Which statement best explains the results?
choices: Natural selection favors allele B in one small population and acts against it in the other.
Mutation rates are higher in small populations than in large ones.
Random changes in allele frequency are larger in small populations and can lead to the loss or fixation of an allele.
Gene flow among the populations keeps the allele frequency constant in the large population.
questions.explanation: Because the allele is neutral, the changes are due to chance, which is genetic drift. In a small population each generation is a small sample of the previous one, so frequencies fluctuate widely and an allele can be lost or fixed. In a large population sampling error is small.

figure.alt: Graph of the percent of bacteria that are resistant over 10 days of growth with an antibiotic: near 1 percent at day 0, about 50 percent at day 4, and close to 100 percent by day 8

questions.stem: A culture of bacteria was grown in the presence of an antibiotic, and the percentage of resistant cells was measured, as shown. Which statement best explains the trend?
choices: A few cells were already resistant, and they survived and reproduced while the susceptible cells died.
The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate in a way that made them resistant.
Individual bacteria gradually adapted to the antibiotic through repeated exposure.
The bacteria used the antibiotic as a nutrient, which let them grow faster.
questions.explanation: Resistance alleles arise by random mutation, independent of the antibiotic. The antibiotic acts as a selective agent: susceptible cells die, and the resistant cells make up a growing share of each generation. The antibiotic does not create the variation it selects.

questions.stem: A river changes course and divides a population of flightless beetles into two groups that can no longer meet. Many generations later the river dries up and the groups come back into contact, but they do not interbreed, because the females of each group respond only to the mating signals of their own males. Which statement best describes what has occurred?
choices: Sympatric speciation, with a postzygotic barrier caused by hybrid sterility
Gene flow between the groups, which made them more similar
Convergent evolution of mating signals in the two groups
Allopatric speciation, with a prezygotic barrier that evolved while the populations were separated
questions.explanation: Geographic isolation stopped gene flow, so the two populations diverged through mutation, selection, and drift. The difference in mating signals is a behavioral barrier that acts before fertilization. Because the groups no longer exchange genes when in contact, they are separate biological species.

rows: Amino acid differences in cytochrome c

figure.alt: Table of amino acid differences in cytochrome c compared with humans: chimpanzee 0, rhesus monkey 1, dog 11, chicken 13, yeast 45

questions.stem: Cytochrome c is a protein of the electron transport chain. The table shows the number of amino acid differences between human cytochrome c and that of other organisms. Which claim is best supported by the data?
choices: Humans evolved from chimpanzees, because the two proteins are identical.
Humans share a more recent common ancestor with rhesus monkeys than with dogs.
Yeast do not share a common ancestor with humans.
Chickens are more closely related to yeast than to humans.
questions.explanation: Differences in a protein's sequence accumulate over time after lineages diverge, so fewer differences indicate more recent common ancestry. All of the organisms have cytochrome c, which is evidence of common ancestry for all of them. Identical proteins show close relationship, not that one living species descended from the other.

questions.stem: Sharks, which are fish, and dolphins, which are mammals, both have streamlined bodies and fins, although their most recent common ancestor had neither feature. Which statement best explains the similarity?
choices: The two groups inherited the features from their most recent common ancestor.
Similar selective pressures in similar environments produced similar adaptations independently.
Dolphins are more closely related to sharks than to other mammals.
The features arose through gene flow between sharks and dolphins.
questions.explanation: Structures that perform the same function but evolved independently are analogous, and the process that produces them is convergent evolution. They do not indicate close relationship. Homologous structures, by contrast, are similar because they were inherited from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: The allele that causes sickle-cell disease in homozygous individuals is found at a high frequency in regions where malaria is common. Which statement best explains this pattern?
choices: The allele is dominant, so it spreads quickly through populations.
Malaria causes the mutation that produces the allele.
Individuals homozygous for the allele have the highest fitness in regions with malaria.
Heterozygous individuals are more likely to survive malaria than individuals homozygous for the normal allele, which keeps both alleles in the population.
questions.explanation: Where malaria is common, heterozygotes have the highest fitness: they are protected against severe malaria and do not have sickle-cell disease. This heterozygote advantage is a form of balancing selection that maintains an allele that is harmful in homozygotes.

figure.alt: Graph of the frequency of the allele for dark wings in a moth population near an industrial city. It rises from about 0.02 in 1850 to about 0.95 by 1900, stays high until the 1950s, and declines after an air-pollution law was passed in 1956, falling to about 0.2 by 2000

questions.stem: The graph shows the frequency of an allele for dark wings in a moth population near an industrial city, where soot darkened tree trunks until air-pollution laws were passed in 1956. Which statement best explains the pattern?
choices: Birds more easily found moths that contrasted with the trunks, so selection favored dark moths while trunks were sooty and light moths after the air was cleaned.
Soot caused mutations for dark wings, and clean air reversed them.
Moths darkened their wings to match the trunks, and passed the change to their offspring.
The pattern resulted from genetic drift, because the allele frequency changed.
questions.explanation: Predators removed the more visible moths, so the better-camouflaged form left more offspring. When the environment changed back, the direction of selection reversed. Drift would not produce a change that tracks pollution in both directions.

figure.alt: Graph of the frequency of the allele for dark wings in a moth population near an industrial city. It rises from about 0.02 in 1850 to about 0.95 by 1900, stays high until the 1950s, and declines after an air-pollution law was passed in 1956, falling to about 0.2 by 2000

questions.stem: A student claims that the rapid rise in the dark-wing allele after 1850 shows that pollution creates the variation that natural selection acts on. Which observation would most directly contradict this claim?
choices: The allele frequency fell after the air-pollution laws were passed.
Light moths were more often eaten by birds on sooty trunks.
Dark moths were found at low frequency in collections made before industrial pollution began.
Dark moths had more offspring than light moths in polluted areas.
questions.explanation: If dark moths existed before pollution, the allele arose by random mutation independent of the environment, and pollution only changed which existing form was favored. The other observations describe selection, not the origin of the variation.

figure.alt: Table of five traits in six organisms. Lancelet: none. Lamprey: vertebral column only. Shark: vertebral column and jaws. Frog: vertebral column, jaws, and lungs. Lizard: those plus an amniotic egg. Mouse: all five, including hair

questions.stem: The table shows the presence of five traits in six organisms. The lancelet is the outgroup. Which organism is most closely related to the lizard?
choices: The frog
The shark
The lamprey
The mouse
questions.explanation: Close relatives share the most derived traits. The lizard and mouse share four derived traits, including the amniotic egg, which no other organism in the table has. That makes them the most recent branch on a tree built from these traits.

figure.alt: Table of five traits in six organisms. Lancelet: none. Lamprey: vertebral column only. Shark: vertebral column and jaws. Frog: vertebral column, jaws, and lungs. Lizard: those plus an amniotic egg. Mouse: all five, including hair

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree built from the table, which trait would appear on the branch leading to the frog, lizard, and mouse but not the shark?
choices: Jaws
The amniotic egg
Lungs
Hair
questions.explanation: A shared derived trait marks the branch where it evolved. Lungs are present in the frog, lizard, and mouse but absent in the shark, so they evolved after the shark's lineage diverged. Jaws are shared with the shark, and the amniotic egg excludes the frog.

figure.alt: Graph of the number of amino acid differences in protein P between pairs of species versus the time since their lineages diverged, as dated by fossils. Five data points fall along a straight line through the origin with a slope of 0.4 differences per million years

questions.stem: The graph relates differences in protein P to divergence times known from fossils. Two living species differ by 30 amino acids in protein P. When did their lineages most likely diverge?
choices: About 30 million years ago
About 75 million years ago
About 12 million years ago
About 120 million years ago
questions.explanation: The line has a slope of 0.4 differences per million years. Dividing 30 differences by 0.4 gives 75 million years. Reading the number of differences as a number of millions of years gives 30.

figure.alt: Graph of the number of amino acid differences in protein P between pairs of species versus the time since their lineages diverged, as dated by fossils. Five data points fall along a straight line through the origin with a slope of 0.4 differences per million years

questions.stem: The method in the graph depends on an assumption. Which assumption is required to use protein P as a molecular clock?
choices: Amino acid changes in protein P accumulate at a roughly constant rate over time.
Protein P is absent from the species being compared.
Protein P is under strong directional selection in every lineage.
Each species has a different version of the genetic code.
questions.explanation: A molecular clock converts the amount of change into time only if change accumulates at a steady average rate. Proteins whose changes are largely neutral are preferred; strong or variable selection would make the rate inconsistent.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 9 percent of individuals show a recessive phenotype. What percentage of the population carries one copy of the recessive allele?
questions.explanation: \(q^2=0.09\), so \(q=0.3\) and \(p=0.7\). Heterozygotes occur at \(2pq=2(0.7)(0.3)=0.42\). The homozygous dominant class is 49 percent.

questions.stem: Which population is most likely to remain close to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for a particular gene?
choices: A very large population with random mating, no migration, and no selection on the gene, in which mutation is rare
A small, isolated population that mates randomly
A large population in which individuals choose mates with the same genotype
A large population that receives many immigrants from a population with different allele frequencies
questions.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires the absence of each evolutionary force: drift (minimized in large populations), gene flow, selection, nonrandom mating, and mutation. Each of the other populations violates one of these conditions.

questions.stem: An unusual form of dwarfism with extra fingers is far more common in one Amish community than in the general population. The community descends from about 200 people who settled together in the 1700s. Which mechanism most likely explains the high frequency?
choices: Natural selection favored the allele in this community.
The allele arises by new mutation in each generation of the community.
Gene flow from neighboring populations introduced the allele.
The founder effect: by chance, one of the original settlers carried the allele, and the small group was isolated afterward.
questions.explanation: When a few individuals start a new population, their alleles may not represent the source population. An allele that is rare elsewhere can become common through this sampling effect and later drift, without any advantage.

questions.stem: Cheetahs have unusually low genetic diversity, so that skin grafts between unrelated cheetahs are often accepted. Which explanation is most consistent with this?
choices: Cheetahs reproduce asexually.
The population was reduced to very few individuals in the past, and the survivors carried only a small part of the original diversity.
Natural selection has favored identical genotypes in all cheetahs.
Cheetahs have an unusually low mutation rate compared with other mammals.
questions.explanation: A bottleneck is a severe reduction in population size that removes many alleles by chance. Even if the population later grows, diversity recovers slowly, which can leave the species vulnerable to disease and environmental change.

questions.stem: Male peacocks have large, conspicuous tails that make them more visible to predators. Which explanation best accounts for the evolution of such a trait?
choices: The tail helps males escape predators by distracting them.
Females prefer to mate with males that have larger tails, so the trait increases reproductive success more than it reduces survival.
The trait arose because males use their tails more than females do.
Large tails evolved because they help regulate body temperature.
questions.explanation: Fitness is measured by reproductive success, not survival alone. Sexual selection can favor traits that are costly for survival when they increase mating success, especially when one sex chooses mates.

questions.stem: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule, which is healthy but sterile. Which type of reproductive barrier keeps horses and donkeys separate species?
choices: A prezygotic barrier: behavioral isolation
A prezygotic barrier: gametic isolation
A postzygotic barrier: reduced hybrid viability
A postzygotic barrier: hybrid sterility
questions.explanation: The barrier acts after fertilization, because a zygote forms and develops into a healthy adult. Because mules cannot reproduce, no genes flow between the two species. Reduced hybrid viability would mean hybrids fail to survive.

questions.stem: Scientists have found that some RNA molecules, called ribozymes, catalyze chemical reactions, including joining nucleotides together. Why is this discovery important to hypotheses about the origin of life?
choices: RNA can both store genetic information and act as a catalyst, so early life could have relied on RNA alone before DNA and proteins.
It shows that the first living cells contained DNA, RNA, and proteins.
It shows that proteins evolved before nucleic acids.
It proves that life arrived on Earth from outer space.
questions.explanation: In modern cells, DNA stores information and proteins catalyze reactions, so each seems to require the other. An RNA world, in which RNA did both jobs, resolves that problem. Ribozymes still form the catalytic core of the ribosome.

figure.alt: Population growth curve: the population starts near 10, increases slowly, then rapidly, passing 250 at about week 5.5, and levels off at about 500 individuals after week 12

questions.stem: The graph shows the growth of a population of insects in a laboratory container with a fixed supply of food added each week. At approximately what population size is the population growing fastest?
choices: 50 individuals
500 individuals
250 individuals
600 individuals
questions.explanation: The rate of population growth is the slope of the curve, which is steepest at the midpoint of the rise, about half the carrying capacity. In logistic growth, \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=r_{\max}N\dfrac{K-N}{K}\) is greatest when \(N=\dfrac{K}{2}\).

figure.alt: Population growth curve: the population starts near 10, increases slowly, then rapidly, passing 250 at about week 5.5, and levels off at about 500 individuals after week 12

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the population shown in the graph levels off at about 500 individuals?
choices: Density-independent factors, such as temperature, increase as the population grows.
The individuals in the population stop reproducing once they reach maturity.
The maximum per capita growth rate of the species increases as the population grows.
Density-dependent factors, such as competition for food, lower the birth rate or raise the death rate as the population grows.
questions.explanation: The container supports a limited number of individuals, its carrying capacity. As density rises, each individual gets a smaller share of the resources, so births decline or deaths increase until the two balance. Density-independent factors affect a population regardless of its size.

questions.stem: A population of 100 fish lives in a pond with a carrying capacity of 500 fish. The maximum per capita growth rate is 0.20 per year. According to the logistic growth model, \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=r_{\max}N\left(\dfrac{K-N}{K}\right)\), what is the current growth rate of the population?
choices: 20 fish per year
80 fish per year
16 fish per year
4 fish per year
questions.explanation: \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=(0.20)(100)\left(\dfrac{500-100}{500}\right)=20(0.8)=16\) fish per year. Twenty per year would be the exponential rate, without the term for the carrying capacity.

figure.alt: Survivorship curves on a logarithmic scale. Species 1 has high survival until late in life, then drops steeply. Species 2 declines at a constant rate. Species 3 drops steeply early in life, and the few survivors then decline slowly

questions.stem: The graph shows survivorship curves for three species. Which description best fits species 3?
choices: It produces few offspring and invests heavily in the care of each one.
It produces very large numbers of offspring and provides little or no parental care.
Individuals have the same chance of dying at every age.
Most individuals survive to old age and then die within a short period.
questions.explanation: The curve for species 3 drops steeply at first, so most individuals die very young, which is typical of organisms such as oysters and many fish and plants that release huge numbers of offspring with no care. Species 1 shows the opposite pattern, and species 2 has a constant death rate.

The rabbit
The frog
The grasshopper
questions.explanation: The hawk is a secondary consumer when it eats rabbits, which eat grass, and a higher-level consumer when it eats snakes. The snake also feeds at two levels. The rabbit and the grasshopper are only primary consumers, and the frog is only a secondary consumer.

questions.stem: A persistent, fat-soluble pollutant is absorbed by the grass in the food web shown. In which organism is the concentration of the pollutant expected to be highest?
choices: The grass
The grasshopper
The hawk
The frog
questions.explanation: Substances that are stored in fat and not excreted accumulate in an organism's tissues. Each consumer eats many organisms from the level below, so the concentration increases at each step of a food chain, a process called biological magnification. Top predators carry the highest concentrations.

questions.stem: Based on the table, what percentage of the energy stored in the biomass of primary consumers is transferred to the biomass of secondary consumers?
questions.explanation: The efficiency is \(\dfrac{240}{2000}=0.12\), or 12%. The transfer from producers to primary consumers in this ecosystem is 10%.

headers: Energy stored in biomass (kJ/m² per year)

figure.alt: Table of energy stored in biomass per square meter per year: producers 20,000 kilojoules, primary consumers 2,000, secondary consumers 240, tertiary consumers 24

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the pattern in the table?
choices: Organisms at higher trophic levels are larger and therefore store less energy.
Energy is recycled from the tertiary consumers back to the producers.
Producers capture less energy than consumers can use.
At each trophic level, most of the energy organisms take in is used in cellular respiration and lost as heat, or is not consumed or assimilated by the next level.
questions.explanation: Energy flows through an ecosystem in one direction. Only the energy stored as new biomass at one level is available to the next; the rest is lost as heat from metabolism or passes to decomposers in wastes and uneaten material. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels.

figure.alt: Graph of two populations over 40 years. The hare population cycles between about 10 and 90 thousand with a 10-year period. The lynx population cycles between about 6 and 38 thousand with the same period, and each lynx peak comes about two years after a hare peak

questions.stem: The graph shows the sizes of a hare population and a lynx population over time. Lynx prey on hares. Which statement best explains why each peak in the lynx population follows a peak in the hare population?
choices: Lynx reproduce only when hares are scarce.
When hares are abundant, more lynx survive and reproduce, and it takes time for those births to raise the lynx population.
Hares reproduce more slowly than lynx.
The lynx population controls the amount of vegetation available to the hares.
questions.explanation: A larger food supply raises the survival and reproduction of the predator, but the predator population responds over a generation, not instantly. As lynx become numerous, predation, along with food shortage for the hares, reduces the hare population, and the lynx then decline in turn.

questions.stem: The table shows the trees in two forest communities. Simpson's diversity index is \(1-\sum\left(\dfrac{n}{N}\right)^2\), where \(n\) is the number of individuals of a species and \(N\) is the total. Which statement is correct?
choices: The communities are equally diverse, because each has four species and 100 trees.
Community 1 is more diverse: its index is 0.75, compared with about 0.27 for community 2.
Community 2 is more diverse, because it has more oak trees.
Community 2 is more diverse: its index is 0.73, compared with 0.25 for community 1.
questions.explanation: For community 1, \(1-4(0.25)^2=0.75\). For community 2, \(1-\left[(0.85)^2+3(0.05)^2\right]=1-0.73=0.27\). The communities have the same species richness, but community 1 has much greater evenness, and diversity depends on both.

questions.stem: On a rocky shore, researchers removed all of the sea stars from one area. The sea stars prey mainly on mussels. Over several years the number of species in the area fell from fifteen to eight, and mussels came to cover most of the rock. Which statement best explains the result?
choices: The sea star is the most abundant species in the community.
Mussels are prey for all of the other species in the community.
Removing any single species from a community reduces its diversity by half.
The sea star is a keystone species whose predation prevents a strong competitor from excluding other species.
questions.explanation: A keystone species has an effect on community structure that is large relative to its abundance. By eating mussels, which are superior competitors for space, the sea star keeps room available for other species. Without it the mussels crowd the others out.

choices: The high dose increased growth relative to the control, and the data do not show a significant effect of the low dose.
Both doses significantly increased growth relative to the control.
Neither dose had a significant effect, because all three means are different.
The low dose significantly increased growth, because its mean is higher than the control's.

figure.alt: Graph of two protist species. Species A grown together with species B increases to about 195 cells per milliliter. Species B grown alone (dashed) increases to about 150. Species B grown together with A increases briefly to about 60 by day 7 and then declines to nearly zero by day 20

questions.stem: Two protist species were grown alone and together in the same medium, as shown. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Species B preys on species A.
The two species can coexist indefinitely in the same container.
When the species share the same limited resources, species A outcompetes species B and drives it nearly to extinction.
Species A depends on species B to survive.
questions.explanation: Species B grows well alone, so the decline is caused by species A. When two species compete for exactly the same resources in the same place, the more efficient competitor eliminates the other, as described by the competitive exclusion principle.

questions.stem: In a separate experiment, the two species shown are grown in a container whose medium is layered so that the top is rich in oxygen and the bottom is rich in bacteria at low oxygen. Both species persist. Which explanation is most consistent?
choices: Species A stops reproducing when species B is present.
The species become a single species when they share a container.
Competition increases when the habitat is more varied.
The species divide the habitat, using different parts of it, so they compete less directly.
questions.explanation: When a habitat offers different resources in different places, competitors can specialize and partition resources. Their realized niches overlap less, so neither excludes the other.

questions.stem: Waterlogged soils have very little oxygen, and nitrogen is lost from them to the atmosphere. Which numbered process in the diagram is most responsible?
choices: Process 1
Process 3
Process 2
Process 4
questions.explanation: Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate instead of oxygen as an electron acceptor in anaerobic conditions, releasing N₂ gas. Nitrification, process 2, requires oxygen and would be slowed in waterlogged soil.

figure.alt: Graph of a lake after fertilizer runoff. Algal biomass rises to a peak of about 10 around day 10 and then falls. Dissolved oxygen stays near 9 to 10 milligrams per liter until about day 12, drops to a minimum of about 2 near day 17, and recovers to 9 by day 30

questions.stem: The graph shows a lake after fertilizer runoff. Which explanation best accounts for the drop in dissolved oxygen around day 17?
choices: Decomposers respiring as they break down the large amount of dead algae consume the oxygen.
The algae consume oxygen as they photosynthesize.
The fertilizer reacts chemically with oxygen in the water.
Fish increase their activity and consume the oxygen.
questions.explanation: Nutrients from the fertilizer cause an algal bloom. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them by aerobic respiration, using oxygen faster than it is replaced. The low point follows the algal peak because decomposition lags the bloom.

questions.stem: Based on the graph, during which period would fish in the lake be most likely to die?
choices: Around day 10, when algal biomass is highest
During the first 5 days, before the bloom begins
Around days 15 to 20, when dissolved oxygen is lowest
After day 25, when dissolved oxygen has recovered
questions.explanation: Fish need dissolved oxygen for aerobic respiration, and the risk is greatest when oxygen is lowest. During the bloom itself, photosynthesis by the algae keeps oxygen high in daylight.

figure.alt: Graph of atmospheric carbon dioxide from 2010 to 2020. The concentration rises from about 389 to about 412 parts per million, with a regular yearly oscillation of about 7 parts per million: each year it peaks in May and reaches a minimum around September and October

questions.stem: The graph shows atmospheric CO₂ measured at a Hawaii observatory. What causes the yearly oscillation?
choices: Photosynthesis by land plants in the Northern Hemisphere removes CO₂ during its summer growing season, and respiration and decomposition release CO₂ in winter.
The oceans release CO₂ every spring and absorb it every fall.
Burning of fossil fuels stops every summer.
Volcanic eruptions in Hawaii occur every spring.
questions.explanation: Most of the land, and therefore most plant biomass, is in the Northern Hemisphere. CO₂ falls from May to about October as plants grow and rises through winter, when respiration exceeds photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which human activity is most responsible for the long-term upward trend shown in the graph?
choices: Increased photosynthesis by crops
Releasing chlorofluorocarbons into the atmosphere
The spread of aerobic respiration among organisms
Burning fossil fuels, which releases carbon that had been stored underground for millions of years
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels contain carbon removed from the active carbon cycle long ago. Burning them adds CO₂ faster than photosynthesis and the oceans remove it. Chlorofluorocarbons damage the ozone layer but do not raise CO₂.

questions.stem: Pond water was sealed in clear and dark bottles and incubated for 24 hours, as shown. What was the gross primary productivity, in milligrams of O₂ per liter per day?
questions.explanation: The dark bottle shows respiration alone: \(8.0-5.0=3.0\) mg/L. The light bottle shows net productivity, photosynthesis minus respiration: \(11.0-8.0=3.0\) mg/L. Gross productivity is the sum, \(3.0+3.0=6.0\), equivalently light minus dark.

questions.stem: Based on the table, which statement about the organisms in the pond water is correct?
choices: They carried out no respiration in the light bottle.
Their net primary productivity was positive, so photosynthesis produced more oxygen than all of the organisms consumed in respiration.
Their net primary productivity was negative, because oxygen fell in the dark bottle.
The data cannot distinguish photosynthesis from respiration.
questions.explanation: Oxygen rose by 3.0 mg/L in the light bottle, where photosynthesis and respiration both occurred, so the community as a whole gained organic matter. Respiration happens in the light as well as in the dark.

questions.stem: An ecosystem's producers store 50,000 kcal per square meter per year in new biomass. If about 10 percent of the energy at each trophic level is transferred to the next, how much energy reaches tertiary consumers?
choices: 500 kcal per square meter per year
5,000 kcal per square meter per year
5 kcal per square meter per year
50 kcal per square meter per year
questions.explanation: Primary consumers receive 5,000, secondary consumers 500, and tertiary consumers 50 kcal per square meter per year. Three transfers separate producers from tertiary consumers.

questions.stem: A plant species introduced to a new continent spreads rapidly and displaces many native plants, although it is uncommon in its native range. Which explanation is most likely?
choices: In its new range it lacks the herbivores, pathogens, and competitors that limited it in its native range.
The plant mutates rapidly after being introduced.
Native plants stop reproducing when a new species arrives.
The new continent has fewer resources than the native range.
questions.explanation: Populations are often held below their potential by natural enemies. An introduced species may escape them, so density-dependent limits are weaker and it can outcompete native species that are still held in check.

questions.stem: Which factor most likely has a greater effect on a population of deer as the population becomes more dense?
choices: A severe winter storm
A forest fire caused by lightning
An infectious disease that spreads by contact between individuals
An unusually long drought
questions.explanation: An infectious disease spreads faster when individuals meet more often, so its effect increases with density, making it a density-dependent factor. Weather events and fires affect a population regardless of its size, so they are density-independent.
